claims.text: Atomic-scale chemical disorder is the primary governor of premelting and melting behavior in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder produces locally variable bonding environments.
Heterogeneous bonding environments create regions with depressed local melting points.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will begin surface premelting earlier than chemically simpler, more uniform nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will have a broader melting-temperature interval than chemically simpler nanoparticles.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are crystalline solid solutions.
The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles possess a high level of atomic-scale chemical disorder.
Intrinsic chemical complexity produces spatial variations in cohesive energy.
Intrinsic chemical complexity produces spatial variations in surface energy.
Regions with lower local melting points initiate premelting at reduced temperatures.
Spatial variation in local melting points broadens the effective nanoparticle melting regime.
Controlled annealing can reduce chemical disorder by promoting local atomic ordering.
Reducing chemical disorder should narrow the melting transition toward that of simpler alloy systems.
The proposed monometallic or lower-entropy baseline nanoparticles have more uniform atomic arrangements.
The proposed chemically simpler baseline nanoparticles have more sharply defined melting transitions.
The proposed mechanism applies to approximately 5-10 nm nanoparticles under inert conditions.
Particle sizes outside the 5-10 nm range may limit the validity of the proposed mechanism.
Oxidizing conditions may introduce surface modifications that limit the validity of the proposed mechanism.
The melting-onset shift and transition broadening may vary with nanoparticle size and composition.
The relative contribution of each constituent element to local disorder is not established.
